Working notes · Susenas September 2025

MBG and poverty: what we did and what we found

The free school meal programme is already counted inside Indonesia's official poverty numbers, but the data does not say which part is the programme. These notes explain how we found it, how much it is worth, and how much poverty it removed.

Data Susenas September 2025, 76,928 households, 283.1 million people Code do\20 to do\24 Status analysis finished; paper not started

01 The problem

Short version: MBG meals are already inside the official poverty numbers. But nothing in the data marks them. So we had to find them.

Susenas asks households about food they ate but did not buy. The enumerator writes down what that food would cost in the local market. MBG meals go into this part of the survey.

From there the meals flow into FOOD, then into EXPEND, then into KAPITA. KAPITA is the number BPS uses to measure poverty. So the poverty rate of 8.25 per cent for September 2025 already includes the meals.

This raises the question we answer here: what would the poverty rate be without MBG? To answer it we must take the meals out. To take them out we must know what they are worth. And the survey never says. Column B41K8 mixes MBG together with food from communal feasts (kenduri), gifts from family, meals at work, and food the household grew.

The hard part

We know exactly who received MBG (question M1106) and how many days (M1108). We do not know how much it was worth. Sections 3 to 6 explain how we found the value without also counting ordinary gifts.

02 What the survey tells us

Short version: 13.6 million people in 10.4 million households received meals in the survey week. Each of those households received about 5.8 meals that week.
13.6 million
people received MBG in the survey week
10.4 million
households with at least one receiver (14.0%)
5.82
meals per household per week
21.5%
of school children received a meal

The MBG questions are in Blok XI of the Modul questionnaire. They ask about each person. The food data is in a different file. The two files join on the household number URUT.

School children are 94 per cent of all receivers. The other groups had barely started: only 2 to 4 per cent of balita, ibu hamil and ibu menyusui received anything. So in practice we are studying a school feeding programme in its first year.

03 Why the simple method fails

Short version: comparing households that received meals with households that did not gives Rp 43,930 per week. But the same comparison also says they received Rp 793 more free cigarettes. No MBG tray has cigarettes.

The first idea is easy. Compare the free food of households that received MBG with the free food of households that did not. Call the difference the programme. For cooked rice meals this gives 59,246 minus 15,316, which is Rp 43,930 per household per week.

This is wrong. MBG goes to households with school children. Those households are different from other households in many ways, and those other ways also change how much free food they get. So the difference mixes the programme with everything else.

How we know it is wrong. Free food received, in rupiah per household per week.
ItemReceived MBGDid notDifferenceWhat it means
Mixed rice plate (nasi campur/rames)59,24615,31643,930Could be the meal
Liquid milk (factory made)3,729913,638Could be the milk
Filter kretek cigarettes (rokok kretek filter)2,2621,469793No MBG tray has cigarettes

Look at the last row. This method says households that received meals also received Rp 793 more free cigarettes. MBG never gives cigarettes. So the method is measuring something that is not the programme. And we cannot tell how much of the Rp 43,930 is that same something.

Two other signs point the same way. Households that received nothing still got Rp 15,316 of free cooked rice, because sharing food is normal in Indonesia. And households with children eat more fruit anyway, whether or not they receive MBG.

04 Our method: compare meals with meals

Short version: we stop comparing receivers with non-receivers. Instead we compare households that received more meals with households that received fewer meals.

If free food really comes from MBG, then a household that gets more meals must get more of that food. Ordinary gifts have no reason to follow the number of meals. So we drop the comparison between receivers and non-receivers, and use only the difference in how many meals each receiving household got.

recdaysi = sum over household members of ( days each one received a meal ) Two children fed four days each gives recdays = 8. The range is 1 to 40. The average is 5.82.
value of item k = ak + bk × recdays + ck × household size + error We use only households that received MBG. b is the rupiah of item k that comes with one more meal.

Three parts make this work:

  • Only receivers. Every household in the test received MBG. So the problem in section 3 cannot happen.
  • The starting value a takes the gifts. Whatever free food these households normally receive goes into a, not into b. That is exactly what the simple method could not remove.
  • We control for household size, because bigger households have more children and eat more of everything.

05 How we checked the method

Short version: we ran the same test on 143 foods that MBG never gives. They all behaved like random noise. The nine MBG foods did not.

One check is not enough. So we ran the same test on every food in the survey, 152 in total. Nine of them turned out to be MBG foods. The other 143 cannot be MBG. If our method is clean, those 143 should show nothing but noise.

How to read this picture

This picture carries most of the weight of our method, so it is worth going through it slowly.

What we did. For every food in the survey we asked the same question: does the free value of this food go up when a household receives more meals? Each answer comes with a number called a t-value. It tells us how far the answer is from zero, measured in standard errors. The bottom axis of the picture shows that number.

Why it works. If a food has nothing to do with MBG, the true answer is zero, and the t-value is only noise. Statistics tells us what noise looks like: centred on zero, and about 95 out of 100 values falling between minus 1.96 and plus 1.96. So we can check the 143 foods against that shape.

What each part of the picture is.
PartMeaning
Blue barsThe 143 foods that are not MBG, sorted by their t-value
Grey curveWhat pure noise should look like
Dashed linesMinus 1.96 and plus 1.96, the usual 5 per cent limits
Orange trianglesThe nine MBG foods, at their own t-values

What we see. The blue bars sit almost on the grey curve. Their average is minus 0.055, and it should be zero. Their spread is 1.084, and it should be 1. About 6.29 per cent go past the dashed lines, and about 5 per cent should. A formal test does not reject the noise shape (p = 0.583).

This is the check that matters. If our meal count were secretly measuring wealth, or measuring how often a household receives gifts, then many foods would move with it. The blue bars would be too wide, or pushed to one side. They are not.

The nine orange triangles sit between t = 3.0 and t = 19.3. They are far outside the range where noise lives. So the nine MBG foods are not lucky results. Noise cannot reach that far.

Two things that confuse people

Some blue bars do pass the dashed lines, and this is correct. Five per cent of pure noise is supposed to pass them. That is what a 5 per cent limit means. Seeing 6.29 per cent agrees with the theory. It is also the reason we do not simply keep every food that passes the 5 per cent test when we choose the nine.

The height of the triangles means nothing. They sit on a line below the axis. Only their left-right position matters. The one at the far right is the mixed rice plate (nasi campur), at t = 19.3. The axis labels stop at 6, so it looks like it is floating at the edge. It is simply very far to the right.

The clearest number

House ownership, building permit, electricity and the education of the household head together explain only 0.2 per cent of the difference in how many meals a household received. One week of meals cannot change any of these four things. So if the meal count were really measuring wealth, these four would predict it. They do not.

One test failed, and we kept it in the report

Coffee and tea moved with the meal count (t = −2.77). We had written down this risk before we ran the test: in Indonesia children drink sweet tea, so coffee and tea are not adult-only foods. This test is therefore not a fair check, and we do not count it as support for the method. We report it because hiding a failed test would be dishonest.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The fruits that appear are the ones you can cut and put on a tray. The other fourteen fruits show nothing. This makes sense, and it tells us the method is finding a real menu and not random foods.

Rp 7,491 against the programme's Rp 10,000

The programme budgets about Rp 10,000 for one portion. Our answer is Rp 7,491, which is three quarters of it. It is tempting to read that as proof that the method works. It is not proof, and this section explains why, because the reason turns out to matter for how the poverty result should be read.

The two numbers measure different things

Rp 10,000 is what the state spends. It covers ingredients, cooking, packing, delivery to the school, and the cost of running the programme.

Rp 7,491 is what the survey records as food in the household. Susenas asks the household to put a rupiah value on food it received without paying. So one number is a cost and the other is a value. There is no rule that says they should be equal.

How Susenas values food that was not bought

BPS tells its enumerators exactly what to do. The manual says that when food comes from own production or as a gift, "perkirakan nilainya dengan harga setempat pada saat barang dikonsumsi" — estimate its value at the local price at the time it was eaten. For cooked food it repeats the instruction: "Bila makanan/minuman jadi yang dikonsumsi berasal dari pemberian, perkirakanlah nilainya sesuai dengan harga setempat."

That second sentence is the one that covers MBG. An MBG meal is cooked food received as a gift, so both the amount and the value go in the gift column, priced at what such a meal costs locally.

We also tested whether enumerators follow the rule. The survey records the quantity of gift food as well as its value, so for a household that both bought and received the same item we can compare the two prices. Across 67,865 such cases the median ratio is 1.000. Food received is valued at the same price the household paid for it. The rule is written down, and it is being applied.

The mistake we made first

Our first explanation of the gap was that cooking, packing and transport sit inside the Rp 10,000 but never arrive as food, so the household value must be lower. That reasoning is wrong.

When you buy a plate of rice at a warung, the price already includes the cooking, the fuel, the packing and the rent. A market price for cooked food is not the price of raw ingredients. Since Susenas values the MBG meal at the local price of such a meal, the kitchen is already inside our Rp 7,491. There is nothing there to subtract.

Very little survives as a real gap between the two numbers. Delivery to the school and the cost of running the programme have no match in a warung price, so those push the cost above the value. But a warung also charges a profit, and the programme does not, which pushes the other way. The two are small and they work against each other.

So what is left to explain the gap?

Three things, and only one of them is a fault in our number.

Why the recorded value is below the programme cost.
ReasonWhat it doesIs our estimate wrong?
The portion is for a childA child's tray is smaller than an adult's plateNo
Children do not finish the foodFood not eaten never becomes household consumptionNo — leaving it out is correct
The mother does not know or does not report what her child ate at schoolFood eaten but never written downYes, and it only pushes the number down

Which makes Rp 7,491 a floor, not a ceiling

This is where the corrected reasoning changes the conclusion. A market price for cooked food is a cost plus a profit. So a full-size MBG portion, fully recorded, valued at local prices, could reasonably come out above Rp 10,000. We measure Rp 7,491.

The item-level numbers say the same thing more sharply. A bought portion of nasi campur has a median value of Rp 11,400. The whole recorded MBG tray — rice, meat or egg, milk and fruit — comes to Rp 7,491, which is 0.66 of one bought plate of rice. The rice part alone is 0.55 of it.

What follows

A tray holding rice, protein, milk and fruit is recorded at two thirds of a single bought plate of rice. Smaller child portions explain some of that. The rest is food the survey does not capture.

So Rp 7,491 is a lowest likely value, and every poverty number built on it is careful rather than large. If the survey captured the whole meal, the poverty effect we report in section 9 would be larger, not smaller.

One thing this comparison cannot do

Rp 7,491 comes out of a regression, not out of an assumption. Nothing in the calculation looks at the Rp 10,000. So the comparison is a fair outside check, and it does tell us something: if the method had returned Rp 800, or Rp 60,000, we would know it was broken. It returned neither.

But it cannot do more than that. Our answer has a 95 per cent range of Rp 6,816 to Rp 8,166. Rp 10,000 sits well outside it, so in a strict statistical sense the two numbers are different, and that tells us nothing at all — they were never supposed to be the same. What makes us trust Rp 7,491 is the testing in section 5, not its distance from the programme budget.

The valuation rule is quoted from BPS, Pedoman Pencacahan Susenas, Modul Konsumsi, kept in reference\BPS_Pedoman_Susenas_2005_konsumsi.pdf. BPS does not publish the current edition; the 2025 questionnaire uses the same columns, and the test above shows the rule is still being applied. The test itself is do\28_unitvalue_check.do, saved as output\mbg_unitvalue_check.csv.

Does the rule for choosing the nine foods matter? Almost not at all.
RuleFoods chosenRp per meal
Plain 5 per cent test107,504
5 per cent test, corrected for testing 152 times (what we use)97,491
A stricter test97,491

The only food in doubt is sweetened condensed milk (susu kental manis), worth Rp 13 per meal. Nothing depends on it.

Does one meal cost more in some regions?

The value of a meal is not the same everywhere: Sumatera 5,893, Jawa 7,487, Bali and Nusa Tenggara 9,535, Kalimantan 9,733, Sulawesi 6,786, Maluku and Papua 9,982. The difference is real (p = 0.0085).

But it does not follow food prices. Sumatera has high food prices and the lowest value. Bali and Nusa Tenggara have low food prices and almost the highest value. So the difference comes from what the kitchens put on the tray, and how well each kitchen was running. It is not a price difference, and we should never call it one.

07 Does MBG replace spending the family would have done anyway?

Short version: we expect some replacement, we cannot measure it well, and every clue we have points to very little. We use ρ = 0 for the headline and carry ρ = 0.25 and ρ = 0.5 beside it.

Why we have to ask

A family gets free meals for its children. Common sense says the family may then buy less food itself. If it does, the meals do not add to what the family consumes. They only take the place of spending that would have happened anyway.

We write this share as ρ. If ρ = 0, the meals add fully. If ρ = 1, the meals only replace, and the programme changes nothing in the survey. Section 9 removes the meals from the data, so it needs a value for ρ. Pick the wrong one and the poverty answer is wrong by the same proportion.

Doing nothing is not an option here. Assuming ρ = 0 without argument would be assuming the answer. So we work through it in four steps: what should decide ρ, what other studies found, how much the answer moves across that range, and what our own data say.

What should decide how big ρ is

Six things decide it. For each one we say where MBG sits.

  1. Does the family already buy more of this food than the meal is worth? If yes, the meal works like cash. The family can move its own money to something else, so its own food spending falls but its total spending does not. If no, the family is pushed to eat more of that food than it wants, and part of the meal is worth less to the family than it cost the state. Our case: every receiving household already buys more food than the meals are worth, Rp 2.93 million a month against Rp 187,000. All of them. So the meal works like cash.
  2. How big is the transfer next to the family budget? Small amounts get spent. Large amounts are more likely to be saved or shared with relatives. Our case: the meals are 3.7 per cent of what a receiving household spends in a month.
  3. If money is freed, where can it go? For ρ to be above zero, the freed money must leave consumption altogether: into saving, into paying back a debt, into money sent to relatives, or into working fewer hours. Nothing else counts, because the survey adds up all consumption, not just food. Our case: families near the poverty line save very little. Debt repayment is real and we do not claim it is zero.
  4. Who eats the meal, and where? A school meal is eaten outside the home. The family may then serve less at home. That is real replacement for the child, but the food saved at home is eaten by someone else in the house. Household consumption is unchanged. Our case: this is why we measure the household, not the child.
  5. Does the family expect the help to last? People save more out of help they think is temporary. Our case: MBG is presented as a permanent national programme.
  6. Labels change behaviour. People treat help labelled "food" differently from cash. They spend more of it on food than they would spend of the same amount in cash. Economists call this the flypaper effect. Our case: MBG is a cooked meal handed to a child at school. It is about as strongly labelled as a transfer can be.
One distinction that decides everything

Most studies measure whether a family buys less of the same food. That is not what we need. Our welfare measure adds up all consumption. If the family buys less rice and more soap, our measure does not change at all.

So a study that finds heavy replacement of own food spending can still mean ρ = 0 for us. The money has to leave consumption entirely before it becomes replacement in our sense. Keep this in mind when reading the table below.

What other studies found

Studies of what families do when they receive food or free schooling. The last column translates each finding into our ρ, which is about total consumption, not food alone.
StudyWhereWhat they foundWhat it means for ρ
Hoynes & Schanzenbach 2009United States, food stampsFamilies already bought more food than the vouchers were worth. They treated one dollar of vouchers like one dollar of cash. Their own food spending fell; their total food spending rose.Near zero for us
Hastings & Shapiro 2018United States, SNAP, shop recordsOut of one dollar of SNAP, 50 to 60 cents went to food. Out of one dollar of cash, much less. Families did not treat the two as the same money.Near zero for us
Kim 2016United States, 2009 benefit riseFamilies spent less of their own money on food and more on rent, transport and school fees.Near zero for us
Jacoby 2002Philippines, school mealsChildren gained almost the full calories of the meal. Families did not take food away from the child. Poorer families took back more than richer ones.Near zero, with a warning about the poorest
Shi 2012China, school fee cutFamilies spent more on the same children, not less.Below zero
Del Ninno & Dorosh 2003Bangladesh, wheat transfersOut of one unit of wheat given, 0.33 showed up as extra wheat eaten. It ranged from about zero for a large work programme to 0.51 for a small school one.Up to two thirds replaced, if the rest left consumption

The pattern is clear in one direction and unclear in the other. Every study finds that this kind of help gets spent rather than saved. No study finds a family that receives food and then consumes less in total. But most of them cannot say where the freed money went, so none of them gives us a number for ρ directly.

Berry and others (2021) also use the words "crowd out" about Indian midday meals, but they mean one school programme pushing out another school programme. That is not household behaviour, so it does not belong in the table above.

So we show the whole range

Because the literature gives a direction and not a number, we do not pick one value and hide the rest. Section 9 recomputes poverty at ρ = 0, ρ = 0.25 and ρ = 0.5, and draws the answer for every value between 0 and 1.

How much the poverty answer moves across the range. National, one value for the country.
ρPoverty removedPeople kept above the lineReading
00.326 pp923,000The meals add fully
0.250.243 pp687,000A quarter is replaced
0.500.158 pp447,000Half is replaced
100The programme changes nothing, by construction

The answer falls roughly in proportion to (1 − ρ). Moving ρ from 0 to 0.5 costs 0.168 percentage points. For comparison, the sampling error at ρ = 0 is 0.174 percentage points. Choosing ρ matters about as much as the size of the survey. That is the reason to take the next step and try to measure it.

Our own check, and what is wrong with it

We can look for ρ in the data itself. Take total spending. Subtract the value of the free MBG food. What is left is the money the household spent itself. Then ask whether households that received more meals spent less of their own money. If the meals change nothing, the answer should be zero.

Read this before the result

It is not an experiment. We compare families that received different numbers of meals in the same week. Nobody handed out those meals at random. We control for what we can see. We cannot control for what we cannot see.

The outcome is the weak kind. In section 5 our checks worked well for food the family was given. They worked less well for things the family bought: one check failed, on tobacco bought with own money. Total spending is a bought-type measure. So this test stands on weaker ground than the meal value in section 6.

There is almost no power. Total household spending swings by about Rp 4.6 million from family to family. The transfer is Rp 31,645. We are looking for something worth 0.7 per cent of the noise around it. Even a true ρ of 0.5 would be hard to see.

So treat what follows as a clue, not as proof.

What the check says

Own spending per one more meal per week. Rupiah per month. The transfer is worth Rp 31,645 per month.

Read the rows from top to bottom. The first row says households that received more meals spent Rp 47,000 more of their own money. A free meal cannot make a family spend more. Something was wrong.

The second row made it worse. We added the share of children, and the number grew to Rp 62,662.

The third row fixed it. We added the share of school-age children, the ones who actually receive the meals, and the number fell to Rp 10,824. The fourth row added province and urban or rural area, and the number fell to Rp 233.

Why the first rows were wrong

Households that receive more meals have more school-age children. Those children cost money: food, clothes, school fees. The first rows counted that spending as if the meals had caused it. When we compare households with the same share of school-age children, living in the same place, the effect disappears.

The answer is Rp 233 per meal, out of a transfer worth Rp 31,645. That is 0.7 per cent. In this sample, households did not cut their own spending. The meals were added on top of what the family already ate. This is the flypaper effect from the list above: help labelled as food is spent on food, not turned into saving.

But the check cannot prove it

The standard error is Rp 27,470, which is large. The true answer could be anywhere between "households spend Rp 54,000 more" and "Rp 54,000 less". In terms of ρ, the range runs from about −1.7 to +1.7.

That range contains 0, 0.25, 0.5 and 1. Our best guess is zero, but this test rules out nothing. All it does is fail to find the large replacement that the naive method seemed to show.

One more thing is worth noticing. Through all four rows, the value of a meal barely moved: 7,491 then 7,384. The own-spending answer moved from 47,009 to 233. Same households, same meal count. Only the thing we were measuring changed. How much free food a family receives does not depend much on how many children it has. How much a family spends in total depends on that very much.

Putting the pieces together

Four separate things now point the same way, and they are not the same evidence counted four times.

  1. Every receiving household is already buying more food than the meals are worth. Rp 2.93 million a month against Rp 187,000. So the meal behaves like cash, and cash of this size gets spent.
  2. Every study in the table finds that this kind of help is spent, not saved. The one closest to MBG, Jacoby on Philippine school meals, finds almost no replacement at all.
  3. Our own check gives 0.7 per cent of the transfer. Weak, but pointing the same way.
  4. Where the poverty answer is decided, saving is smallest. For ρ to be above zero, the money must leave consumption. Families just under the poverty line save very little. Whatever ρ is on average, it should be smaller among exactly those families.
So the headline uses ρ = 0

Section 9 and section 10 report ρ = 0 as the headline. That is a choice, and here is the whole reason for it: it is the value our own data give, it is the value the literature points to, and it is the value that fits how big the transfer is next to what these families already buy.

It is not a claim that ρ is zero. We cannot show that. What we can show is that no evidence we have points anywhere else. So the tables carry ρ = 0.25 and ρ = 0.5 in the columns beside the headline, every time, and the reader should carry them too.

08 Who receives MBG

Short version: more in urban than in rural areas, and about the same across rich and poor. Poor rural families are 26 per cent of the children who should get meals but receive 16 per cent of them.

This is what a first year looks like. Kitchens opened first where they were easiest to run. It matters for the next section: help that misses the poorest removes less poverty than the same money would if it reached them.

09 How much poverty it removed

Short version: about 923,000 people were kept above the poverty line in that week. Without MBG the poverty rate would have been 8.58 per cent instead of 8.25 per cent.
First we checked our own code

We measured poverty using the BPS KAPITA and got 8.2524, 6.5996 and 10.7176 for the country, urban and rural areas, and Gini 0.36285, 0.38318 and 0.29525. These are the published numbers exactly. The code stops itself if they do not match. So everything below starts from a correct base.

0.326
percentage points removed from the poverty rate
923,257
people kept above the poverty line
±0.087
range of error, 95 per cent
Why the headline uses ρ = 0

ρ is the share of the meals that only replaced spending the family would have done anyway. We set it to zero. Section 7 works through that choice in full: what should decide ρ, what other studies found, and what our own data say. The short reason is that all three point the same way, and none of them points anywhere else.

Section 7 also shows that our own measurement is weak. Its range covers ρ = 0.5 and more. So the table below gives the answer at ρ = 0.25 and ρ = 0.5 as well. Both belong to the result. Reporting only ρ = 0 would claim more knowledge than we have.

Result under each way of valuing meals and each level of replacement. The first column is the headline. The other two are the sensitivity check, not alternatives we believe equally.

Urban and rural areas

MBG removes more poverty in urban areas: 0.381 percentage points, against 0.244 in rural areas. Both are clear. This follows from section 8. Three quarters of receivers live in urban areas, so that is where the effect appears, even though rural poverty is much higher (10.72 against 6.60 per cent). The programme is strongest where poverty is smallest.

10 How much of the fall in poverty does MBG explain?

Short version: almost all of it. Poverty fell from 8.57 per cent in September 2024 to 8.25 per cent in September 2025. Without MBG it would have been 8.58 per cent, which is the same as a year earlier. The fall would not have happened.

Section 9 gives the size of the MBG effect in one month. This section puts that size next to the change BPS reported over time. The two are different things and we keep them apart. Our number compares September 2025 with and without MBG. The BPS number compares September 2025 with an earlier month, when everything else was also different.

8.25
poverty rate, September 2025, published
8.58
poverty rate, September 2025, if MBG were removed
8.57

The levels, side by side

Made by do\25_mbg_trend_chart.do; also saved as output\mbg_contribution_to_decline.csv. Published levels from BPS, Profil Kemiskinan di Indonesia September 2025 (BRS No. 19/02/Th. XXIX), Tabel 1 and Tabel 6.

Urban and rural areas tell different stories

In urban areas, poverty barely moved over the year: 6.66 per cent down to 6.60 per cent. The number of poor urban people actually rose, from 11.05 juta to 11.18 juta. Without MBG the urban rate would have been 6.98 per cent, which is 0.32 points above where it started. MBG is the reason urban poverty did not rise.

In rural areas, poverty fell a lot: 11.34 per cent down to 10.72 per cent. MBG explains 39 per cent of that fall. Something else did most of the work. BPS points to the rice harvest: the harvested area in September 2025 was 9.71 per cent larger than a year before, and production 8.74 per cent larger.

This changes how to read section 8

Section 8 showed that MBG reaches urban areas far more than rural areas, and called this a weakness in aim. That is still true. But the two facts sit together in an interesting way: the meals went to the place that had no other help, while rural areas were helped by the harvest.

This is not a defence of the targeting. The same money aimed at poor rural families would have removed more poverty, because more of them sit just below the line. It only means the programme happened to cover a gap.

How much of this survives a higher ρ?

The share of the fall that MBG explains, at three values of ρ.
ρMBG effectShare of the fall since Sep 2024Share of the fall since Mar 2025
0 (headline)0.326 pp102%148%
0.250.243 pp76%110%
0.500.158 pp49%72%

The strongest claim, that poverty would not have fallen at all, needs ρ near zero. The weaker claim survives much further. For any ρ below about 0.32, poverty in September 2025 would still have been above its March 2025 level. And even at ρ = 0.5, MBG explains about half the fall since September 2024.

Three things this is not

1. It is not a decomposition. We compare September 2025 with and without MBG in the same month. The change over a year mixes everything: prices, wages, work, the harvest, other help. A share of 102 per cent means that everything else together did about nothing to measured poverty over the year. It does not mean nothing else happened.

2. MBG already existed in March 2025. The programme started in January 2025 and grew all year, so part of its effect is already inside the March 2025 figure. Our calculation removes all of MBG from September, not only the part added since March. The March comparison therefore claims too much. September 2024 is the clean comparison, because MBG did not exist then. This is why we lead with it.

3. March and September are different seasons. The two rounds fall at different points of the farming year. BPS compares one year to the same month a year before for this reason. That is a second reason to lead with September 2024.

One thing worth noticing

The BRS lists nine reasons for the September 2025 poverty figure: growth of 5.04 per cent, 1.90 juta more people in work, a larger rice harvest, and social assistance of Rp 112.7 triliun. MBG is not on the list.

The social assistance figure is worth a second look. It grew 1.0 per cent in rupiah over the year. The poverty line grew 7.76 per cent. So the older programmes bought less than they did a year before. MBG is the part of the system that grew.

11 What could the same money have done?

Short version: given as cash to the poorest fifth of households, the same money would remove 1.21 percentage points of poverty instead of 0.33. But only if it reached them. Delivered as well as Indonesia's cash programmes deliver today, it removes 0.44.

MBG is not a cash programme, and nobody proposed it as one. But it spends real money, and that money could have been spent another way. This section asks a simple question: if the government had handed out the same amount as cash, how much poverty would it have removed?

The rule of the exercise

Every design below spends exactly the same amount: Rp 1.83 trillion a month. That is the value of the MBG food that reached households, from section 6. It is not the programme's budget, which is larger, because part of the budget pays for kitchens and delivery and never arrives on a plate.

We do not fix the amount each household gets. We fix the total. So the amount per household is the budget divided by the number of households that receive it. A design that reaches few households pays each of them more.

We rank households by their spending per person without MBG, measured in units of their own poverty line. A household in Jakarta and one in rural Nusa Tenggara with the same rupiah are not equally poor, because prices differ, so we use the poverty line BPS sets for each province and for urban and rural areas separately.

Aiming tighter is worth a lot

Compare the three perfect-aim designs. Giving everyone the same money removes 0.098 points. Giving it to the poorest 40% removes 0.432. Giving it to the poorest 20% removes 1.214.

Two things happen at once when the target narrows. Fewer households share the money, so each gets more. And more of the money lands on households that are actually poor. Cash to everyone fails on both counts: Rp 24,589 a month is about Rp 6,500 per person, against a poverty line of Rp 641,443. That is one per cent of the line. Almost nobody crosses it.

The cost tells the same story. Cash to everyone costs Rp 6.6 million for each person kept above the line. Cash to the poorest fifth costs Rp 532,000 — twelve times cheaper for the same result.

But delivering it is worth more

The finding

Aimed perfectly, moving the rule from the poorest 40% to the poorest 20% almost triples the effect: 0.432 to 1.214 points.

Delivered the way these programmes actually deliver, the same move gains almost nothing: 0.429 to 0.439 points. Narrowing the rule buys 0.010 points. The other 0.775 points sit behind delivery, not behind the rule.

The two programmes are damaged very differently. BPNT delivering a bottom-40 rule loses almost nothing: 0.429 against 0.432, under one per cent. PKH delivering a bottom-20 rule loses 64 per cent of what the rule could do.

The reason is leakage. PKH reaches 10.97 million households, but only 3.79 million of them are in the poorest fifth. The other 7.18 million are outside it, which is the 65.5 per cent in the table above. A narrow target is fragile. The same amount of misdirected money does far more damage when the group you are aiming at is small.

What this means for policy

A government that wants more poverty reduction from the same budget has two levers: write a tighter eligibility rule, or reach the people the rule names.

These numbers say the second lever is the one that matters. With today's delivery, tightening the rule from 40 per cent to 20 per cent is almost worthless. Fixing who actually receives is worth up to 0.78 percentage points of poverty — more than twice what MBG itself removes.

Where MBG sits

MBG removes 0.326 points. That is more than three times what the same money would do handed to everyone, and about three quarters of what cash to the poorest 40% would do. It costs Rp 1.98 million per person lifted, against Rp 1.50 million for bottom-40 cash and Rp 532,000 for bottom-20 cash.

One difference is worth noting. MBG is the only design here that does more in urban than in rural areas: 0.381 against 0.244. Every cash design does more in rural areas, because rural households sit lower on the ranking once prices are taken into account. Cash to the poorest fifth removes 1.67 points in rural areas against 0.91 in urban areas.

This is not an argument that MBG should have been cash. MBG is meant to feed children and help them learn, and this page measures none of that. What the comparison shows is the price of the choice, measured in one thing only: poverty in the month we can see.

Five things this is not

1. Cash goes per household, not per person. A family of seven gets the same as a family of two, so it gets less per person. A per-person rule would give different answers.

2. We assume the cash is fully spent. This is the same assumption we make for MBG at ρ = 0, so the two are compared on equal terms. If people save part of the cash, every cash number here is too high.

3. Nobody pays for administration. Not for MBG's kitchens, not for a cash system's registry and transfers. Both are free in this exercise, which they are not in life.

4. We copy the error rates, not the reasons for them. A household left out by BPNT in real life is left out every month, because it is missing from the register. In our draw it gets a fresh chance each time. Real exclusion sticks; ours does not.

5. The survey is not the register. 15.4 million households say they received BPNT. The programme's quota is about 18 million families, and a household can hold more than one family. These are different things counted in different ways.

Made by do\26_mbg_cash_scenarios.do and do\27_mbg_cash_chart.do; results in output\mbg_cash_scenarios.csv, the 600 random draws in output\mbg_cash_mc.csv. The budget is checked against Rp 1,829,580,543,779 in every design and in every draw, and the code stops if it ever differs by more than one part in ten thousand.

12 Inequality and cost

Short version: MBG moves poverty but not inequality. It costs about Rp 2 million per month for each person kept above the line.

The change in the Gini is 0.0016, which is almost nothing. This is expected. The meals are worth 3.7 per cent of what a receiving household spends, and receivers are spread across rich and poor families. To move inequality a programme must be both large and well aimed at the poor.

Cost for each person kept above the poverty line, per month, when ρ = 0.
Value usedTotal per monthPeopleRp per person

A value for each regionRp 1,805 billion885,4122,038,217
Full programme costRp 2,387 billion1,290,8741,849,191

This is a simple division, not a judgement about whether the programme is good value. MBG is meant to feed children and help them learn. Removing poverty is a side effect. Comparing this number with a cash programme would not be fair to MBG.

13 What is strong and what is weak

Short version: the meal value and the poverty numbers are strong. The replacement share ρ and the fact that we only have one week are weak.
StatementHow strongWhy
Our base matches BPS exactlyCertainThe code checks it and stops if it fails
Rp 7,491 for one mealStrong143 other foods show nothing; the answer barely moves when we change the controls or the choosing rule
About 923,000 people kept above the lineStrongError range 0.239 to 0.413 points; holds under every way of valuing meals
Effect is larger in urban than in rural areasStrongClear gap, and it agrees with who receives the meals
Urban poverty would have risen without MBGStrongUrban poverty fell only 0.06 points over the year while MBG removed 0.38; the gap is far larger than the error range
Cash to the poorest fifth would remove far more povertyStrong1.214 against 0.326 points, same budget; holds on every measure and in both urban and rural areas
Delivery matters more than the eligibility ruleStrongTightening from 40% to 20% gains 0.010 points once real coverage rates are applied; the other 0.775 sits behind delivery
MBG explains the whole fall since September 2024MediumTrue at ρ = 0, which is our own estimate. At ρ = 0.5 it explains about half. It is a comparison of two numbers, not a decomposition
Households do not cut their own spendingWeakBest guess is zero, but the error range covers everything
Meal value differs by regionMediumThe difference is real, but our reason for it is a guess
This describes MBG in generalNoOne week only, first year, 14 per cent of households

Four things to remember

  • The meals are already in the official numbers. We are not measuring what MBG did to families. We are measuring how much of the published 8.25 per cent comes from counting the meals.
  • We never remove more than a household reported. If we skip this rule the answer becomes 0.351 instead of 0.326 points, which is 7 per cent too high.
  • Poverty lines stay the same in both cases, and each household is judged against the line of its own province and its own urban or rural area. This is what BPS does, and it is why our base matches theirs.
  • The survey does show kabupaten (all 514 of them). We found this late. It opens the door to comparing areas if we can get an earlier round of the survey.

The longer write-up for a paper is a separate file, output\mbg_methodology.html. This page is the simple version. The Stata results for each number are on this page, inside the boxes marked Show the Stata output.

If you come back to this later

  • Everything runs on the original BPS files. The file we rebuilt ourselves is only proof that our sums are right. Never use it in the analysis.
  • Two Stata problems cost us time. A temporary file made inside a program disappears when the program ends. And export delimited writes the words, not the numbers, so reading the file back gives text.
  • Still to do: the paper outline, one more robustness test, and an error range for the Gini change.
